title: Microsoft finally admits Windows 11 needs a serious cleanup, but the update is for developers only
excerpt: A stripped-back Windows 11 build tuned for developers, shipping pinned VS Code, Windows Terminal with runtimes.
content_html:
Published Sep 4, 2026, 2:48 PM EDT

Hamed holds a B.A. in English Literature, graduating cum laude. He loves music, tech gadgets, and exploring the latest in the world of LLMs. He also enjoys tinkering with creative software such as Logic Pro, Final Cut Pro, and Photoshop.

A lifelong musician, Hamed plays multiple instruments, including guitar, bass, and oud. He is equally fascinated by smart-home technology and can happily spend hours geeking out over connected lights, speakers, sensors, and automations that make everyday life a little more interesting. When he isn’t covering the latest tech news, he explores more creative topics on his Medium blog, works on his music, or clears his head by riding his motorcycle.

Summary

  • Project Zenith is a ready-to-code Windows 11 experience, decluttered and preconfigured with dev tools like VS Code and Terminal.
  • It comes preinstalled on AMD Ryzen AI Halo PCs with at least 64GB unified memory and 250GB/s bandwidth.
  • It's not a new version, but rather a preconfigured Windows 11; most settings are replicable via Windows Developer Config.

The market for LLM-capable computers is hot, as we've previously seen with a surge in local LLM builds on Apple Silicon Mac Minis. Now Microsoft is targeting developers and people handling demanding AI workloads with Project Zenith, hoping to strengthen Windows’ appeal as an alternative to macOS-based development setups. Project Zenith is a new “ready-to-code” Windows 11 experience designed to remove distractions and come preconfigured with tools developers would typically install themselves.

According to Microsoft’s official announcement, Project Zenith will first become available on devices powered by AMD Ryzen AI Halo before expanding to hardware from other chipmakers and PC manufacturers. Despite the badass name, Project Zenith is not a new Windows edition. It is still the same Windows 11 available elsewhere; Microsoft and its hardware partners simply configure it differently before handing it to the buyer.

A Windows 11 with some sensible defaults

But only reserved for exceptionally powerful PCs

In order to qualify to run Project Zenith, a PC must come with at least 64GB of unified memory and 250GB/s of memory bandwidth. Microsoft says that hardware will let developers run AI models with more than 30 billion parameters locally without burning through cloud tokens.

The interesting part, however, is what Microsoft has done to Windows itself. With Project Zenith preconfigurations, File Explorer shows file extensions, hidden files, the complete folder path, and its "Details" pane by default. Long-path support is enabled, and things like recently used files and sync-provider tips are toggled off.

What’s more, Microsoft enables Command Palette and disables Start menu tips and account notifications. I think this is Microsoft finally admitting that Windows 11 feels better with some of its annoying features removed. You can already make the regular Start menu considerably cleaner by disabling every suggestion, but Zenith machines ship that way.

Other changes include Windows Terminal and Visual Studio Code being pinned to the taskbar. You can also expect runtimes, source-control utilities, and some other developer tools preinstalled on Zenith. PowerToys is a worthy mention in the list of preinstalled tools, especially as Microsoft continues giving it quality-of-life features that Windows itself still lacks.

Project Zenith also fits a wider cleanup effort inside Microsoft. The company recently stripped unnecessary tools from the Windows 11 Photos viewer to make it faster and less distracting. That said, limiting its most thoughtfully configured Windows experience to premium developer hardware is a rather odd choice when the clutter has nothing to do with RAM or memory bandwidth.

The good news is that you don't actually need a Project Zenith flagship computer to reproduce most of its software experience. Microsoft’s open-source Windows Developer Config uses WinGet Configuration to install common development tools, configure WSL, enable developer-focused features, and turn off several Windows distractions on pretty much any PC.
